claim: Human visual performance is better at the fovea than at peripheral locations.
source: Performance is better at the fovea, decreases with eccentricity
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a general characterization of visual performance across the visual field.

claim: Human visual performance decreases with increasing eccentricity.
source: Performance is better at the fovea, decreases with eccentricity
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is a well-established finding in vision science.

claim: Visual performance is better along the horizontal meridian than the vertical meridian.
source: Performance is better at the fovea, decreases with eccentricity, and is better along the horizontal than vertical meridian and along the lower than the upper vertical meridian.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of polar angle asymmetries.

claim: Visual performance is better along the lower vertical meridian than the upper vertical meridian.
source: Performance is better at the fovea, decreases with eccentricity, and is better along the horizontal than vertical meridian and along the lower than the upper vertical meridian.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of polar angle asymmetries.

claim: Most performance differences due to eccentricity are eliminated when stimulus size is cortically magnified (M-scaled) to equate the size of its cortical representation in primary visual cortex (V1).
source: Most performance differences due to eccentricity are eliminated when stimulus size is cortically magnified (M-scaled) to equate the size of its cortical representation in primary visual cortex (V1).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations to prior work in the introduction.

claim: M-scaling stimulus size eliminates differences in contrast sensitivity across eccentricity.
source: We found that although M-scaling stimulus size eliminates differences across eccentricity, it does not eliminate differences around the polar angle.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in the results.

claim: M-scaling stimulus size does not eliminate differences in contrast sensitivity around polar angle.
source: We found that although M-scaling stimulus size eliminates differences across eccentricity, it does not eliminate differences around the polar angle.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data presented in the results.

claim: Limits in contrast sensitivity across eccentricity and around polar angle of the visual field are mediated by different anatomical and computational constraints.
source: This finding indicates that limits in contrast sensitivity across eccentricity and around polar angle of the visual field are mediated by different anatomical and computational constraints.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract, inferred from the differential effects of M-scaling on eccentricity versus polar angle.

claim: Contrast sensitivity is bandpass near the fovea, peaking at approximately 4 cycles per degree.
source: Contrast sensitivity, a fundamental visual capability, is bandpass near the fovea, peaking at ~4 cycles per degree (cpd) (Campbell and Robson, 1968; Watson and Ahumada, 2005)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Campbell and Robson, 1968 and Watson and Ahumada, 2005.

claim: Contrast sensitivity declines with eccentricity.
source: Contrast sensitivity, a fundamental visual capability, is bandpass near the fovea, peaking at ~4 cycles per degree (cpd) (Campbell and Robson, 1968; Watson and Ahumada, 2005), and declines with eccentricity (Hilz and Cavonius, 1974; Robson and Graham, 1981; Wright and Johnston, 1983).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Hilz and Cavonius, 1974; Robson and Graham, 1981; Wright and Johnston, 1983.

claim: Contrast sensitivity is higher along the horizontal than vertical meridian (horizontal-vertical anisotropy, HVA).
source: Contrast sensitivity also varies around polar angle: it is higher along the horizontal than vertical meridian – horizontal-vertical anisotropy (HVA) – and along the lower than upper vertical meridian – vertical meridian asymmetry (VMA) (Abrams et al., 2012; Baldwin et al., 2012; Cameron et al., 2002; Carrasco et al., 2022; Carrasco et al., 2001; Hanning et al., 2022a; Hanning et al., 2022b; Himmelberg et al., 2022b; Himmelberg et al., 2020; Pointer and Hess, 1989; Rosén et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Contrast sensitivity is higher along the lower than upper vertical meridian (vertical meridian asymmetry, VMA).
source: Contrast sensitivity also varies around polar angle: it is higher along the horizontal than vertical meridian – horizontal-vertical anisotropy (HVA) – and along the lower than upper vertical meridian – vertical meridian asymmetry (VMA) (Abrams et al., 2012; Baldwin et al., 2012; Cameron et al., 2002; Carrasco et al., 2022; Carrasco et al., 2001; Hanning et al., 2022a; Hanning et al., 2022b; Himmelberg et al., 2022b; Himmelberg et al., 2020; Pointer and Hess, 1989; Rosén et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Contrast asymmetries depend upon stimulus eccentricity.
source: These contrast asymmetries depend upon stimulus eccentricity (Carrasco et al., 2001; Hilz and Cavonius, 1974; Himmelberg et al., 2020; Robson and Graham, 1981; Wright and Johnston, 1983)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Contrast asymmetries depend upon spatial frequency.
source: These contrast asymmetries depend upon stimulus eccentricity (Carrasco et al., 2001; Hilz and Cavonius, 1974; Himmelberg et al., 2020; Robson and Graham, 1981; Wright and Johnston, 1983), spatial frequency (SF) (Baldwin et al., 2012; Cameron et al., 2002; Campbell and Robson, 1968; Carrasco et al., 2001; Himmelberg et al., 2020; Rovamo et al., 1992)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Contrast asymmetries depend upon stimulus size.
source: These contrast asymmetries depend upon stimulus eccentricity (Carrasco et al., 2001; Hilz and Cavonius, 1974; Himmelberg et al., 2020; Robson and Graham, 1981; Wright and Johnston, 1983), spatial frequency (SF) (Baldwin et al., 2012; Cameron et al., 2002; Campbell and Robson, 1968; Carrasco et al., 2001; Himmelberg et al., 2020; Rovamo et al., 1992), and size (Himmelberg et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Himmelberg et al., 2020.

claim: Perceptual polar angle asymmetries can be as pronounced as doubling stimulus eccentricity.
source: Perceptual polar angle asymmetries can be as pronounced as doubling stimulus eccentricity (Carrasco et al., 2001; Himmelberg et al., 2020)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Carrasco et al., 2001 and Himmelberg et al., 2020.

claim: Perceptual polar angle asymmetries persist across different stimulus orientations.
source: They persist across different stimulus orientations (Baldwin et al., 2012; Carrasco et al., 2001; Corbett and Carrasco, 2011)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Perceptual polar angle asymmetries persist across different eccentricities and spatial frequencies.
source: They persist across different stimulus orientations (Baldwin et al., 2012; Carrasco et al., 2001; Corbett and Carrasco, 2011), eccentricities and SFs (Barbot et al., 2021; Cameron et al., 2002; Carrasco et al., 2001; Himmelberg et al., 2020; Rijsdijk et al., 1980)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Perceptual polar angle asymmetries persist across different luminance levels.
source: They persist across different stimulus orientations (Baldwin et al., 2012; Carrasco et al., 2001; Corbett and Carrasco, 2011), eccentricities and SFs (Barbot et al., 2021; Cameron et al., 2002; Carrasco et al., 2001; Himmelberg et al., 2020; Rijsdijk et al., 1980), luminance levels (Carrasco et al., 2001)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Carrasco et al., 2001.

claim: Perceptual polar angle asymmetries persist across head rotations.
source: They persist across different stimulus orientations (Baldwin et al., 2012; Carrasco et al., 2001; Corbett and Carrasco, 2011), eccentricities and SFs (Barbot et al., 2021; Cameron et al., 2002; Carrasco et al., 2001; Himmelberg et al., 2020; Rijsdijk et al., 1980), luminance levels (Carrasco et al., 2001), head rotations (Corbett and Carrasco, 2011)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Corbett and Carrasco, 2011.

claim: Perceptual polar angle asymmetries persist across different stimulus sizes.
source: They persist across different stimulus orientations (Baldwin et al., 2012; Carrasco et al., 2001; Corbett and Carrasco, 2011), eccentricities and SFs (Barbot et al., 2021; Cameron et al., 2002; Carrasco et al., 2001; Himmelberg et al., 2020; Rijsdijk et al., 1980), luminance levels (Carrasco et al., 2001), head rotations (Corbett and Carrasco, 2011), and sizes (Himmelberg et al., 2020)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Himmelberg et al., 2020.

claim: Perceptual polar angle asymmetries persist in the presence of distractors.
source: They persist across different stimulus orientations (Baldwin et al., 2012; Carrasco et al., 2001; Corbett and Carrasco, 2011), eccentricities and SFs (Barbot et al., 2021; Cameron et al., 2002; Carrasco et al., 2001; Himmelberg et al., 2020; Rijsdijk et al., 1980), luminance levels (Carrasco et al., 2001), head rotations (Corbett and Carrasco, 2011), and sizes (Himmelberg et al., 2020), in the presence of distractors (Carrasco et al., 2001; Purokayastha et al., 2021)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Carrasco et al., 2001 and Purokayastha et al., 2021.

claim: Perceptual polar angle asymmetries persist across manipulations of covert attention.
source: They persist across different stimulus orientations (Baldwin et al., 2012; Carrasco et al., 2001; Corbett and Carrasco, 2011), eccentricities and SFs (Barbot et al., 2021; Cameron et al., 2002; Carrasco et al., 2001; Himmelberg et al., 2020; Rijsdijk et al., 1980), luminance levels (Carrasco et al., 2001), head rotations (Corbett and Carrasco, 2011), and sizes (Himmelberg et al., 2020), in the presence of distractors (Carrasco et al., 2001; Purokayastha et al., 2021), across manipulations of covert attention (Cameron et al., 2002; Carrasco et al., 2001; Purokayastha et al., 2021; Roberts et al., 2018; Roberts et al., 2016; Talgar and Carrasco, 2002)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Perceptual polar angle asymmetries persist across manipulations of presaccadic attention.
source: They persist across different stimulus orientations (Baldwin et al., 2012; Carrasco et al., 2001; Corbett and Carrasco, 2011), eccentricities and SFs (Barbot et al., 2021; Cameron et al., 2002; Carrasco et al., 2001; Himmelberg et al., 2020; Rijsdijk et al., 1980), luminance levels (Carrasco et al., 2001), head rotations (Corbett and Carrasco, 2011), and sizes (Himmelberg et al., 2020), in the presence of distractors (Carrasco et al., 2001; Purokayastha et al., 2021), across manipulations of covert attention (Cameron et al., 2002; Carrasco et al., 2001; Purokayastha et al., 2021; Roberts et al., 2018; Roberts et al., 2016; Talgar and Carrasco, 2002) and presaccadic attention (Hanning et al., 2022a; Hanning et al., 2022b)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Hanning et al., 2022a and Hanning et al., 2022b.

claim: Perceptual polar angle asymmetries persist under monocular and binocular viewing conditions.
source: They persist across different stimulus orientations (Baldwin et al., 2012; Carrasco et al., 2001; Corbett and Carrasco, 2011), eccentricities and SFs (Barbot et al., 2021; Cameron et al., 2002; Carrasco et al., 2001; Himmelberg et al., 2020; Rijsdijk et al., 1980), luminance levels (Carrasco et al., 2001), head rotations (Corbett and Carrasco, 2011), and sizes (Himmelberg et al., 2020), in the presence of distractors (Carrasco et al., 2001; Purokayastha et al., 2021), across manipulations of covert attention (Cameron et al., 2002; Carrasco et al., 2001; Purokayastha et al., 2021; Roberts et al., 2018; Roberts et al., 2016; Talgar and Carrasco, 2002) and presaccadic attention (Hanning et al., 2022a; Hanning et al., 2022b), as well as under monocular and binocular viewing conditions (Barbot et al., 2021; Carrasco et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Barbot et al., 2021 and Carrasco et al., 2001.

claim: Perceptual asymmetries are retinotopic rather than spatiotopic.
source: Importantly, the perceptual asymmetries are retinotopic rather than spatiotopic; when observers rotate their head, the asymmetries shift in line with the retinal location of the stimulus rather than their location in space (Corbett and Carrasco, 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Corbett and Carrasco, 2011.

claim: Perceptual asymmetries have been related to optical factors.
source: These asymmetries have been related to optical (Kupers et al., 2019), retinal (Kupers et al., 2022), and cortical factors (Benson et al., 2021; Himmelberg et al., 2023a; Himmelberg et al., 2022b, Himmelberg et al., 2021; Silva et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Kupers et al., 2019.

claim: Perceptual asymmetries have been related to retinal factors.
source: These asymmetries have been related to optical (Kupers et al., 2019), retinal (Kupers et al., 2022), and cortical factors (Benson et al., 2021; Himmelberg et al., 2023a; Himmelberg et al., 2022b, Himmelberg et al., 2021; Silva et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Kupers et al., 2022.

claim: Perceptual asymmetries have been related to cortical factors.
source: These asymmetries have been related to optical (Kupers et al., 2019), retinal (Kupers et al., 2022), and cortical factors (Benson et al., 2021; Himmelberg et al., 2023a; Himmelberg et al., 2022b, Himmelberg et al., 2021; Silva et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cortical magnification is the amount of cortical surface area corresponding to one degree of visual angle (mm²/°).
source: Cortical magnification –the amount of cortical surface area corresponding to one degree of visual angle (mm2/°) – declines with eccentricity (Benson et al., 2022; Engel et al., 1994; Himmelberg et al., 2021; Horton and Hoyt, 1991; Van Essen et al., 1984)
evidence: This is a definition provided in the introduction.

claim: Cortical magnification declines with eccentricity.
source: Cortical magnification –the amount of cortical surface area corresponding to one degree of visual angle (mm2/°) – declines with eccentricity (Benson et al., 2022; Engel et al., 1994; Himmelberg et al., 2021; Horton and Hoyt, 1991; Van Essen et al., 1984)
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Cortical magnification has been used to link perceptual performance to brain structure.
source: Cortical magnification –the amount of cortical surface area corresponding to one degree of visual angle (mm2/°) – declines with eccentricity (Benson et al., 2022; Engel et al., 1994; Himmelberg et al., 2021; Horton and Hoyt, 1991; Van Essen et al., 1984) and has been used to link perceptual performance to brain structure (Duncan and Boynton, 2003; Himmelberg et al., 2023a; Himmelberg et al., 2022b; Rovamo et al., 1978; Schwarzkopf et al., 2011; Schwarzkopf and Rees, 2013; Song et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: For many visual tasks, magnifying stimulus size such that the spatial extent of the cortical representation is equated eliminates performance differences at different eccentricities.
source: Indeed, for many visual tasks (e.g., contrast sensitivity, orientation and SF discrimination, grating acuity, temporal frequency sensitivity, and visual search), magnifying stimulus size such that the spatial extent of the cortical representation is equated eliminates performance differences at different eccentricities (Figure 1A; Anton-Erxleben and Carrasco, 2013; Carrasco et al., 1998; Carrasco and Frieder, 1997; Kitterle, 1986; Rovamo and Virsu, 1979; Strasburger et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Grating contrast sensitivity as a function of spatial frequency successfully scales with eccentricity.
source: Particularly relevant to this study, grating contrast sensitivity as a function of SF successfully scales with eccentricity (Hilz and Cavonius, 1974; Koenderink et al., 1978; Rovamo et al., 1978; Virsu and Rovamo, 1979).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by multiple citations.

claim: The decline in performance with eccentricity is due to decreasing neural count with eccentricity (quantitative hypothesis).
source: These studies support a 'quantitative' hypothesis – the hypothesis that the decline in performance with eccentricity is due to decreasing neural count with eccentricity, given that the density, but not distribution, of V1 neurons is approximately uniform across cortex (and thus visual space) (Hubel and Wiesel, 1977; Rockel et al., 1980).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Hubel and Wiesel, 1977 and Rockel et al., 1980.

claim: The density, but not distribution, of V1 neurons is approximately uniform across cortex.
source: These studies support a 'quantitative' hypothesis – the hypothesis that the decline in performance with eccentricity is due to decreasing neural count with eccentricity, given that the density, but not distribution, of V1 neurons is approximately uniform across cortex (and thus visual space) (Hubel and Wiesel, 1977; Rockel et al., 1980).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Hubel and Wiesel, 1977 and Rockel et al., 1980.

claim: The quantitative hypothesis suggests that visual processing is invariant with location; neurons conduct the same computations, regardless of their receptive field position.
source: This hypothesis then suggests that visual processing is invariant with location; neurons conduct the same computations, regardless of their receptive field position.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an implication of the quantitative hypothesis.

claim: Performance does not successfully scale for several visual tasks measuring higher-order dimensions (e.g., numerosity judgments, symmetry detection, and positional relation of image components).
source: Indeed, performance does not successfully scale for several visual tasks measuring higher-order dimensions (e.g., numerosity judgments, symmetry detection, and positional relation of image components; for review, see Strasburger et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by a citation to Strasburger et al., 2011.

claim: Observers performed an orientation discrimination task with constant stimulus size at different locations.
source: Here, to assess contrast sensitivity, human adult observers performed an orientation discrimination task with constant stimulus size at different locations as well as when stimulus size was M-scaled according to stimulus eccentricity and polar angle location.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a description of the experimental design.

claim: Observers performed an orientation discrimination task when stimulus size was M-scaled according to stimulus eccentricity and polar angle location.
source: Here, to assess contrast sensitivity, human adult observers performed an orientation discrimination task with constant stimulus size at different locations as well as when stimulus size was M-scaled according to stimulus eccentricity and polar angle location.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a description of the experimental design.

claim: Ten observers with normal or corrected-to-normal vision participated in three conditions.
source: Ten observers with normal or corrected-to-normal vision participated in three conditions (eight females, aged 21–32 y, two authors: MJ and DT).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section describing the participants.

claim: Observers maintained fixation during the task.
source: While maintaining fixation, observers reported the orientation of a target grating for which contrast and spatial frequency (SF) varied on each trial (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the experimental procedure.

claim: Grating contrast and spatial frequency varied on each trial.
source: While maintaining fixation, observers reported the orientation of a target grating for which contrast and spatial frequency (SF) varied on each trial (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the experimental procedure.

claim: CSFs decline between the parafovea (2°) and perifovea (6°) for fixed-sized gratings.
source: CSFs decline between the parafovea (2°) and perifovea (6°) for fixed-sized gratings (top row), but differences at low and medium SFs diminish after M-scaling Virsu and Rovamo, 1979 (bottom row).
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1 and shown in the figure.

claim: Differences in CSFs at low and medium spatial frequencies diminish after M-scaling.
source: CSFs decline between the parafovea (2°) and perifovea (6°) for fixed-sized gratings (top row), but differences at low and medium SFs diminish after M-scaling Virsu and Rovamo, 1979 (bottom row).
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1 and shown in the figure, with citation to Virsu and Rovamo, 1979.

claim: CSFs differ among the horizontal meridian (HM), lower vertical meridian (LVM), and upper vertical meridian (UVM) for fixed-sized stimuli.
source: CSFs differ among the horizontal meridian (HM), lower vertical meridian (LVM), and upper vertical meridian (UVM) for fixed-sized stimuli (top row).
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 1B and shown in the figure.

claim: Contrast sensitivity peaked at a given spatial frequency and declined more rapidly for higher than lower spatial frequencies.
source: Contrast sensitivity peaked at a given SF and declined more rapidly for higher than lower SFs.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the shape of the CSF.

claim: CSFs decreased with eccentricity but less so after M-scaling.
source: CSFs decreased with eccentricity but less so after M-scaling.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The eccentricity effect for fixed-size gratings increased from approximately 30% to 120% across spatial frequency.
source: The eccentricity effect for fixed-size gratings, quantified as the percent change in contrast sensitivity for 2°, 6°, and 6°M-scale, increased from ~30% to 120% across SF (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: After M-scaling, the eccentricity effect became negative for spatial frequencies less than 2 cpd, with higher contrast sensitivity at 6° M-scale than 2°.
source: After M-scaling, the eccentricity effect became negative for SFs <2 cpd, with higher contrast sensitivity at 6°M-scale than 2° (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: M-scaling diminished the eccentricity effect differentially across spatial frequency.
source: A repeated-measures ANOVA (SF: 0.5–11 cpd; stimulus size: fixed vs. M-scaled) showed that M-scaling diminished the eccentricity effect differentially across SF (interaction: F(7,63) = 61.13, p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.872).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical test results.

claim: M-scaling resulted in significant reductions in contrast sensitivity for spatial frequencies 0.5, 1, 1.4, 2, 2.8, and 4 cpd.
source: Post hoc t-tests revealed significant reductions in contrast sensitivity for all SFs (0.5, 1, 1.4, 2, and 2.8 cpd, p<0.001; 4, cpd, p<0.01) except the two highest SFs (8 and 11 cpd, p>0.1), which reached the acuity limit.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical test results.

claim: M-scaling did not result in significant reductions in contrast sensitivity for spatial frequencies 8 and 11 cpd, which reached the acuity limit.
source: Post hoc t-tests revealed significant reductions in contrast sensitivity for all SFs (0.5, 1, 1.4, 2, and 2.8 cpd, p<0.001; 4, cpd, p<0.01) except the two highest SFs (8 and 11 cpd, p>0.1), which reached the acuity limit.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical test results.

claim: M-scaling slightly reversed typical eccentricity effects for low spatial frequencies.
source: Thus, consistent with previous results (Rovamo et al., 1978; Rovamo and Virsu, 1979), M-scaling slightly reversed typical eccentricity effects for low SFs and reduced them for medium SFs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1, with citations to prior work.

claim: M-scaling reduced eccentricity effects for medium spatial frequencies.
source: Thus, consistent with previous results (Rovamo et al., 1978; Rovamo and Virsu, 1979), M-scaling slightly reversed typical eccentricity effects for low SFs and reduced them for medium SFs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1, with citations to prior work.

claim: Contrast sensitivity across spatial frequencies was greater for the horizontal meridian than vertical meridian at 2°, 6°, and 6° M-scale.
source: Contrast sensitivity across SFs was greater for the HM than VM at 2°, 6°, and 6°M-scale (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: At 2° and 6°, the HVA extent increased from 20% to 120% across spatial frequency.
source: At 2° and 6°, the HVA extent increased from 20% to 120% across SF (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Differences in contrast sensitivity between the horizontal meridian and vertical meridian at a fixed eccentricity were as pronounced as tripling stimulus eccentricity from 2° to 6°.
source: Thus, differences in contrast sensitivity between the HM and VM at a fixed eccentricity were as pronounced as tripling stimulus eccentricity from 2° to 6°.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a comparison of the magnitude of HVA to eccentricity effects.

claim: The HVA remained after M-scaling.
source: The HVA remained after M-scaling.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: M-scaling the stimulus reduced the HVA extent as a function of spatial frequency.
source: A two-way ANOVA compared its extent at the perifovea (6° eccentricity) before and after M-scaling. M-scaling the stimulus reduced the HVA extent as a function of SF (interaction: F(7,63) = 7.32, p=0.0035, ηG2 = 0.449).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical test results.

claim: For all but one spatial frequency (8 cpd), M-scaling did not affect the HVA.
source: For all but one SF (8 cpd: p=0.021, 95% CI = [1.26 57.37], d = 0.75), M-scaling did not affect the HVA (p>0.05).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical test results.

claim: Unlike eccentricity, the HVA must be mediated by factors beyond cortical magnification, such as qualitatively different image-processing capabilities and/or neural computations around polar angle.
source: This finding supports the 'qualitative' hypothesis – unlike eccentricity, the HVA must be mediated by factors beyond cortical magnification, such as qualitatively different image-processing capabilities and/or neural computations around polar angle (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the finding that M-scaling does not eliminate the HVA.

claim: Contrast sensitivity across spatial frequencies was higher along the lower vertical meridian than upper vertical meridian for 2°, 6°, and 6° M-scale.
source: Contrast sensitivity across SFs was higher along the LVM than UVM for 2°, 6°, and 6°M-scale (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: For fixed-size and M-scaled gratings, the VMA extent reached a maximum of 40% at 1 cpd in the parafovea and 8 cpd in the perifovea.
source: For fixed-size and M-scaled gratings, the VMA extent reached a maximum of 40% at 1 cpd in the parafovea and 8 cpd in the perifovea.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section.

claim: The VMA has only been characterized at eccentricities greater than 2°.
source: The VMA has only been characterized at eccentricities > 2° (Abrams et al., 2012; Cameron et al., 2002; Carrasco et al., 2001; Himmelberg et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with citations to prior work.

claim: The spatial frequency at which the VMA peaks depends on eccentricity.
source: This near-foveal location reveals that the SF at which the VMA peaks depends on eccentricity.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the data showing different peak SFs for VMA at different eccentricities.

claim: The VMA remained after M-scaling.
source: The VMA also remained after M-scaling (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and shown in Figure 4F.

claim: A two-way ANOVA found a main effect of spatial frequency on VMA extent.
source: A two-way ANOVA found a main effect of SF (F(7,63) = 10.16, p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.53) due to an increasing perifoveal VMA extent across SF.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical test results.

claim: There was no main effect of stimulus size on VMA extent.
source: We found neither a main effect of stimulus size nor an interaction effect (p>0.1), indicating no difference in VMA extent before and after M-scaling stimulus size.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical test results.

claim: There was no interaction effect between stimulus size and spatial frequency on VMA extent.
source: We found neither a main effect of stimulus size nor an interaction effect (p>0.1), indicating no difference in VMA extent before and after M-scaling stimulus size.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical test results.

claim: Unlike eccentricity, the VMA must be mediated by factors beyond cortical magnification, such as distinct neural computations and image-processing capabilities at the upper vertical meridian and lower vertical meridian.
source: This finding further supports the 'qualitative' hypothesis – unlike eccentricity, the VMA must be mediated by factors beyond cortical magnification, such distinct neural computations and image-processing capabilities at the UVM and LVM (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an interpretation of the finding that M-scaling does not eliminate the VMA.

claim: The HVA in peak contrast sensitivity emerged only in the perifovea.
source: The HVA emerged in the peak-CS only in the perifovea (interaction: F(2,18) = 18.33, p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.671; Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical test results and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Peak contrast sensitivity fell between 2° and 6° for both HVA and VMA.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical test results.

claim: Peak contrast sensitivity increased in the perifovea after M-scaling for both HVA and VMA.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with statistical test results.

claim: Peak contrast sensitivity did not differ between 2° and 6° M-scale.

claim: M-scaling stimulus size based on the cortical representation as a function of polar angle had no effect on the VMA.
source: Together, these novel findings support the 'qualitative' hypothesis. M-scaling stimulus size based on the cortical representation as a function of polar angle diminished – but did not eliminate – the HVA, and had no effect on the VMA.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the findings.

claim: Performance differences as a function of polar angle are likely to be mediated by both the cortical representation and by differential computations or image-processing capabilities of these neurons.
source: These findings suggest that performance differences as a function of polar angle are likely to be mediated by both the cortical representation and by differential computations or image-processing capabilities of these neurons (i.e., differently tuned spatial filters).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Observers' viewing distance changed when the stimuli were presented at the horizontal meridian and the vertical meridian for the non-scaled stimulus size.
source: We note that observers' viewing distance changed when the stimuli were presented at the HM and the VM for the non-scaled stimulus size.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a methodological note.

claim: The change in viewing distance changed monitor luminance (23 cd/m² and 19 cd/m², respectively).
source: This change in distance changed monitor luminance (23 cd/m2 and 19 cd/m2, respectively).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a methodological note.

claim: The change in luminance is not large enough to significantly affect contrast measurements.
source: However, this change in luminance is not large enough to significantly affect contrast measurements (Rahimi-Nasrabadi et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation to Rahimi-Nasrabadi et al., 2021.

claim: Asymmetries in contrast sensitivity have been reported in many studies for which the viewing distance has been constant.
source: Moreover, these asymmetries in contrast sensitivity have been reported in many studies for which the viewing distance has been constant (Abrams et al., 2012; Baldwin et al., 2012; Barbot et al., 2021; Cameron et al., 2002; Carrasco et al., 2022; Carrasco et al., 2001; Hanning et al., 2022a; Himmelberg et al., 2022b; Himmelberg et al., 2020; Pointer and Hess, 1989; Regan and Beverley, 1983; Rijsdijk et al., 1980; Robson and Graham, 1981; Rosén et al., 2014; Silva et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Perceptual asymmetries have been linked to V1 properties (surface area, population receptive field size, and BOLD amplitude) at the group level.
source: Perceptual asymmetries have been linked to the V1 properties (surface area, population receptive field [pRF] size, and BOLD amplitude) at the group- (Benson et al., 2021; Himmelberg et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2006; Moutsiana et al., 2016; O'Connell et al., 2016; Silva et al., 2018) and individual level (Himmelberg et al., 2022b).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by multiple citations.

claim: Perceptual asymmetries have been linked to V1 properties at the individual level.
source: Perceptual asymmetries have been linked to the V1 properties (surface area, population receptive field [pRF] size, and BOLD amplitude) at the group- (Benson et al., 2021; Himmelberg et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2006; Moutsiana et al., 2016; O'Connell et al., 2016; Silva et al., 2018) and individual level (Himmelberg et al., 2022b).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by a citation to Himmelberg et al., 2022b.

claim: Individual differences in contrast sensitivity correlate with individual differences in V1 surface area along the polar angle meridians.
source: Further, here we show that individual differences in contrast sensitivity in our own data correlate with individual differences in V1 surface area along the polar angle meridians.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the findings.

claim: The asymmetries must be explained by cortical magnification to some extent.
source: Thus, the asymmetries must be explained by cortical magnification to some extent.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as an inference from the correlation findings.

claim: M-scaling has been shown to work for fundamental visual dimensions.
source: M-scaling has been shown to work for fundamental visual dimensions (Cowey and Rolls, 1974; Di Russo et al., 2005; Himmelberg and Wade, 2019; Levi et al., 1999; Ludvigh, 1941; Rovamo et al., 1978; Virsu et al., 1982; Virsu and Rovamo, 1979; Wertheim, 1894)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by multiple citations.

claim: M-scaling has been shown to fail for other visual dimensions, typically (but not always) more complex dimensions.
source: M-scaling has been shown to work for fundamental visual dimensions (Cowey and Rolls, 1974; Di Russo et al., 2005; Himmelberg and Wade, 2019; Levi et al., 1999; Ludvigh, 1941; Rovamo et al., 1978; Virsu et al., 1982; Virsu and Rovamo, 1979; Wertheim, 1894) – and fail for others, typically (but not always) more complex dimensions (Hilz et al., 1981; Levi and Klein, 1986; Solomon and Sperling, 1995; Strasburger et al., 1994; Strasburger et al., 1991; Tyler, 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by multiple citations.

claim: For the same visual task and dimension, M-scaling stimulus size works for certain locations – eccentricity – but fails for others – cardinal polar angles.
source: Critically, here we found that for the same visual task and dimension, M-scaling stimulus size works for certain locations – eccentricity – but fails for others – cardinal polar angles.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a summary of the main finding.

claim: Between-subject variability in the V1 polar angle representation may underlie the inability of M-scaling to extinguish perceptual polar angle asymmetries.
source: One possibility is that between-subject variability in the V1 polar angle representation underlies the inability of M-scaling to extinguish perceptual polar angle asymmetries.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a possible explanation.

claim: There is substantial variability in the size of V1.
source: There is substantial variability in the size of V1 (Benson et al., 2022; Dougherty et al., 2003; Himmelberg et al., 2022b; Moutsiana et al., 2016)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by multiple citations.

claim: There is substantial variability in how V1 tissue is distributed throughout the visual field.
source: There is substantial variability in the size of V1 (Benson et al., 2022; Dougherty et al., 2003; Himmelberg et al., 2022b; Moutsiana et al., 2016) and how V1 tissue is distributed throughout the visual field (Benson et al., 2022; Himmelberg et al., 2023a; Himmelberg et al., 2022b).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by multiple citations.

claim: There may be greater variability in the cortical representation of polar angle compared to eccentricity that is not accounted for by the M-scaling equations derived from group-level data.
source: Another possibility is that there is greater variability in the cortical representation of polar angle compared to eccentricity that is not accounted for by the M-scaling equations that were derived from group-level data (Rovamo and Virsu, 1979).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a possible explanation, with citation to Rovamo and Virsu, 1979.

claim: Even if stimulus size were adjusted via M-scaling equations based on individualized V1 surface measures, the perceptual asymmetries would likely remain.
source: This suggests that even if stimulus size were adjusted via M-scaling equations based on individualized V1 surface measures, the perceptual asymmetries would likely remain.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section as a speculation based on the lack of correlation between V1 surface area and the change in contrast sensitivity after M-scaling.

claim: Limits in contrast sensitivity across eccentricity and around polar angle likely emerge from different anatomical and computational constraints.
source: These findings reveal that limits in contrast sensitivity across eccentricity and around polar angle likely emerge from different anatomical and computational constraints
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as the main conclusion of the study.

claim: The findings challenge the generalizability of the established view that cortical magnification limits basic visual perception throughout the visual field.
source: These findings reveal that limits in contrast sensitivity across eccentricity and around polar angle likely emerge from different anatomical and computational constraints, and challenge the generalizability of the established view that cortical magnification limits basic visual perception throughout the visual field (Duncan and Boynton, 2003; Rovamo and Virsu, 1979; Schwarzkopf et al., 2011; Schwarzkopf and Rees, 2013; Song et al., 2015; Virsu and Rovamo, 1979).
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Differences in contrast sensitivity at different eccentricities are predominantly mediated by cortical magnification.
source: Although differences in contrast sensitivity at different eccentricities are predominantly mediated by cortical magnification, differences as a function of polar angle must be constrained by additional computational and neural image-processing capabilities.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as a summary of the findings.

claim: Differences in contrast sensitivity as a function of polar angle must be constrained by additional computational and neural image-processing capabilities.
source: Although differences in contrast sensitivity at different eccentricities are predominantly mediated by cortical magnification, differences as a function of polar angle must be constrained by additional computational and neural image-processing capabilities.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as a summary of the findings.

claim: Models of spatial vision linking brain and behavior should account for what constrains basic visual perception not only across – but also around – the visual field.
source: Models of spatial vision linking brain and behavior should account for what constrains basic visual perception not only across – but also around – the visual field.
evidence: This is stated in the Conclusions section as a recommendation for future modeling work.

claim: Sinusoidal gratings with spatial frequencies of 0.5, 1, 1.4, 2, 2.8, 4, 8, or 11.3 cpd served as targets.
source: Sinusoidal gratings with an SF of 0.5, 1, 1.4, 2, 2.8, 4, 8, or 11.3 cpd served as targets.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section describing the stimuli.

claim: For the horizontal meridian condition, stimuli appeared along the left and right horizontal meridian at 2° and 6° eccentricity.
source: For the HM condition, stimuli appeared along the left and right HM at 2° and 6° eccentricity.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section describing the stimuli.

claim: For the vertical meridian condition, stimuli appeared at 2° and 6° eccentricity along the upper and lower vertical meridian.
source: Similarly, stimuli appeared at the same eccentricities but along the upper and LVM for the VM condition.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section describing the stimuli.

claim: During the horizontal meridian and vertical meridian conditions, a two-dimensional cosine function (4° wide, centered on the grating's peak luminance) windowed each grating at 2° and 6° eccentricity.
source: During the HM and VM conditions, a two-dimensional cosine function (4° wide, centered on the grating's peak luminance) windowed each grating at 2° and 6° eccentricity.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section describing the stimuli.

claim: For the M-scale condition, gratings appeared at 6° eccentricity along horizontal meridian and vertical meridian.
source: For the M-scale condition, gratings appeared at 6° eccentricity along HM and VM.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section describing the stimuli.

claim: Grating sizes were scaled separately for each polar angle, based on meridian-dependent M-scaling equations.
source: We scaled grating sizes separately for each polar angle, based on meridian-dependent M-scaling equations (Rovamo and Virsu, 1979)
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section describing the stimuli, with citation to Rovamo and Virsu, 1979.

claim: M-scaled gratings subtended 7.68° for the lower vertical meridian, 7.70° for the upper vertical meridian, and 7.08° for the horizontal meridian.
source: We scaled grating sizes separately for each polar angle, based on meridian-dependent M-scaling equations (Rovamo and Virsu, 1979), resulting in gratings that subtended 7.68° for the LVM, 7.70° for the UVM, and 7.08° for the HM.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section describing the stimuli.

claim: If the eye blinked or deviated more than 1° from fixation, the trial was immediately aborted and rerun at the end of the block.
source: If the eye blinked or deviated >1° from fixation, the trial was immediately aborted and rerun at the end of the block.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section describing the behavioral protocol.

claim: Observers received auditory feedback for incorrect responses on a trial-by-trial basis.
source: They received auditory feedback for incorrect responses on a trial-by-trial basis.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section describing the behavioral protocol.

claim: For the horizontal meridian condition, observers completed 1080 trials per location (left and right horizontal meridian; 160 trials per spatial frequency).
source: For the HM condition, they completed 1080 trials per location (left and right HM; 160 trials per SF)
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section describing the procedure.

claim: For the vertical meridian condition, observers completed 1344 trials per location (upper vertical meridian and lower vertical meridian; 140 trials per spatial frequency).
source: for the VM condition 1344 per location (UVM and LVM; 140 trials per SF)
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section describing the procedure.

claim: For the M-scale condition, observers completed 1008 trials per location (84 trials per spatial frequency).
source: and for the M-scale condition 1008 per location (84 trials per SF).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section describing the procedure.

claim: For vertical meridian and M-scale conditions, contrast was titrated separately for each combination of spatial frequency, eccentricity, and polar angle with best PEST, a maximum likelihood adaptive procedure.
source: For VM and M-scale conditions, we titrated contrast separately for each combination of SF, eccentricity, and polar angle with best PEST, a maximum likelihood adaptive procedure, using custom code (https://github.com/michaeljigo/palamedes_wrapper; Jigo, 2021) that ran subroutines implemented in the Palamedes toolbox (Prins and Kingdom, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section describing the titration procedure.

claim: For the horizontal meridian condition, a 3-down, 1-up weighted staircase was used.
source: For HM, we used a 3-down, 1-up weighted staircase (García-Pérez, 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section describing the titration procedure, with citation to García-Pérez, 1998.

claim: Both titration procedures targeted 75% task performance.
source: Both titration procedures targeted 75% task performance.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section describing the titration procedure.

claim: The parametric model includes a logistic function for the contrast response function, with slope fixed across spatial frequency.
source: Our model includes (1) a logistic function for the CRF, with slope fixed across SF (Jigo and Carrasco, 2020) and asymptotes matched to the specifications of the adaptive titration procedure
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section describing the parametric contrast sensitivity model, with citation to Jigo and Carrasco, 2020.

claim: Nine candidate models of the contrast sensitivity function were tested.
source: Our model includes (1) a logistic function for the CRF, with slope fixed across SF (Jigo and Carrasco, 2020) and asymptotes matched to the specifications of the adaptive titration procedure; (2) nine candidate models of the CSF
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section describing the parametric contrast sensitivity model.

claim: Six visual field models were tested that specify how contrast sensitivity changes with eccentricity and polar angle.
source: Our model includes (1) a logistic function for the CRF, with slope fixed across SF (Jigo and Carrasco, 2020) and asymptotes matched to the specifications of the adaptive titration procedure; (2) nine candidate models of the CSF; and (3) six visual field models that specify how contrast sensitivity changes with eccentricity and polar angle.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section describing the parametric contrast sensitivity model.

claim: Model fitting was performed at the group level.
source: We performed model fitting at the group level and in two stages to (1) identify the best-fitting CSF model and (2) determine the appropriate visual field model.
evidence: This is stated in the Methods section describing the model fitting procedure.

claim: The best-fitting CSF model was the YQM model.
source: The bolded entry indicates the best-fitting model.
evidence: This is indicated in Table 1 where the YQM model is bolded, and shown in Figure 3A where it has the lowest ΔBIC value.

claim: The best-fitting visual field model was 'Ecc + HVA + VMA'.
source: The bolded entry indicates the best-fitting model.
evidence: This is indicated in Table 2 where the 'Ecc + HVA + VMA' model is bolded, and shown in Figure 3B where it has the lowest ΔBIC value.

claim: Seven of the ten observers had fMRI-derived retinotopic maps.
source: Here, we measured the distribution of V1 surface area at the polar angle meridians and confirmed that individual measurements of V1 surface area correlate with contrast sensitivity across our observers. We correlated the amount of V1 surface area representing ±15° wedge-ROIs (1–8° of eccentricity) centered along the HM, UVM, and LVM of the visual field with the respective peak-CS measurement at 2°, 6°, and 6°M-scale for 7 of our 10 observers for whom we could obtain fMRI-derived retinotopic maps.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the fMRI analysis.
